subject: ventures/vending-machine-planogram-optimizer
professional: an independent vending route operator who sets planograms for snack, drink and fresh-food machines; they check first whether fast movers get facings in proportion to velocity so nothing sells out before the next fill, whether par levels (including underfilled coils for fresh food) match the fill frequency and shelf life, what each slot earns in margin after commission and card fees, and whether coil capacity is respected

evidence.correctness: The engine is right for its stated model. python3 -I /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-oss-monorepo/70bb90b8-d3c5-5c45-9e48-64fa9ddb24f9/scratchpad/vending/indep.py (own Poisson pmf via lgamma, greedy marginal allocation, which is exact for this separable concave objective, own RNG Monte Carlo) reproduces the example: allocation [8,4,6,5,3,3,4,2,1], $254.3304/week vs calc.mjs analyticGross 254.3304; even split 204.0087 vs 204.0087; potato chips E[min(D,80)] at lambda 70 = 69.4897 and P(D>=80) = 12.91% (page: 69.5, 13%); the restock table at 2/7/10/14 days nets $137.87/$224.33/$205.82/$158.84, identical to the page; an independent MC without substitution gives $254.26. A Python brute force over every allocation (bf.py on 40 random 3-4 product machines from bf.mjs, with perishables, min and max coils and 2-10 day gaps) finds 0 mismatches with optimize(). A hand check of substitution (soda 400/wk on 8x15 coils, water 20/wk, 30% switch) gives a $70.4/week gap; the tool shows -$70.27. Held at 2 by two outputs a user acts on: (1) a blank 'Max coils' silently becomes 8 (calc.mjs:93), so a 40-coil drink machine with soda at 400/week and water at 20/week is told to use 12 of 40 coils, soda sells out 100% of intervals, and 'One more coil ... $0.00 a week ... The machine has more coils than the products can use well' (page loaded in Chrome via Playwright); (2) because the optimiser ignores substitution, its 'best split' can be significantly worse than the layout it is compared with (-$70.27 +/- 0.22 a week on explicit max 8/8, 16 coils, 30% switching).
evidence.completeness: Claimed features all run end to end: exact DP split with min/max, sell-out percentage per product, value of one more and one fewer coil, restock-gap table for 2-14 days net of visit cost, paired Monte Carlo against today's layout or an even split with standard error, perishable waste, CSV download, usage opt-out, deterministic results. Loaded index.html from a local static server in headless Chrome (Playwright, 390 px wide): example renders, no console errors, scrollWidth 390. No TODOs or stubs. The served page https://marisstella.app/vending-machine-planogram-optimizer/ could not be fetched (proxy CONNECT 403), so the deploy-time version was not compared.
evidence.verification: cd ventures/vending-machine-planogram-optimizer && node --test '*.test.mjs': 26 tests, 26 pass (251 ms); bare `node --test` as the README says also runs 26 on Node 22.23.4. The brute-force and Poisson-sum tests are genuinely independent and good. Seven mutations via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: 1 caught (perishable waste priced at price not cost in visitProfit), 6 survived: weekly scaling 7/interval -> 7/(interval+1) (every headline weekly dollar 12.5% low), sell-out probability index off by one, extra-coil value computed with the same coil count (always $0), visit cost charged once a week in the restock table regardless of gap, perishable waste dropped from the simulation, default max coils 8 -> 4. Only the DP objective is pinned; nearly every displayed number other than the allocation is unguarded.
evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs (285 lines, pure functions, clear DP with backtrack, exact Poisson tail sums, seeded RNG, common random numbers), index.html module script (escapes product names with esc() before innerHTML), usage.mjs (guarded storage, DNT/GPC). Defects: undisclosed magic default of 8 for a blank max (calc.mjs:93); fewerCoil returns Infinity and renders '$Infinity a week' when minimum coils fill the machine (calc.mjs:259; edge.mjs: 2 products, min 2 each, 4 coils); num() strips every comma so a decimal-comma price '1,50' becomes 150 with no warning (calc.mjs:32); page.test.mjs calls the sibling route-margin tool 'a sibling restaurant tool'.
evidence.claims: Disclaimer, no-upload privacy, local-only counters and DNT honoured: backed by index.html footer and usage.mjs, and page.test.mjs checks the event names. 'Exact' split: backed for the model (brute force agrees). 'The optimiser itself ignores substitution, so it can only understate the value of the layout' (README.md:17, index.html:113 'so it can only understate'): false; with substitution the recommended split can lose to the comparison layout (-$70.27/week shown above), and the page then prints 'earns less than the comparison' with no explanation. 'Get the split of coils that earns the most' is not true when Max coils is left blank (silent cap of 8, not stated on the page). '30 is typical for snacks' (index.html substitution note) has no source. Limits (coil types, shelf life, commissions, card fees, seasonality) are stated in README and the page's 'Not decided'. llms.txt points at the github.io address; the build rewrites hosts at deploy, so not filed (source-only).
evidence.fitness: Walked the operator's job: a 36-coil snack machine with nine SKUs and last month's sales, explicit min/max set. The tool gives a sensible split (chips 8, chocolate 6, trail mix 1), sell-out risk per SKU and the restock gap, which an operator could act on. It breaks on common cases: a drink machine with few SKUs and blank max coils is told to leave most coils empty; fresh food can only be loaded in full coils (no par level), so a sandwich at 6/week in an 8-unit coil earns $6.47/week where a par of 5 earns $9.15 (newsvendor, indep.py); margin per slot is before location commission and card-reader fees (stated), which an operator always nets out; one machine at a time, no route-level fill planning or pick list.
evidence.domain: Compared against the standard newsvendor/marginal-facing method (allocate the next facing where expected margin gain is largest, Poisson demand per fill cycle) and route practice of setting pars against fill frequency: the core method matches and an operator would recognise the 'value of one more coil' and visit-cost trade-off. Departures: no par level below coil capacity, which is how fresh food is actually stocked; no shelf-life constraint, so a 7-day example cycle, and a 14-day row in the restock table, are computed for fresh sandwiches without a warning; Poisson demand with no overdispersion understates sell-outs for event- and weekday-driven locations; substitution is used only to grade the result, not to choose it; margin ignores commission and card fees (stated).

defects.what: A blank 'Max coils' silently becomes 8, so on a large or few-SKU machine the 'best split' leaves coils empty while a best seller sells out every interval, and the page then advises that the machine has more coils than the products can use (40 coils, soda 400/wk: [8,4], 28 empty, extra coil $0.00). The default is not stated on the page.

README and page claim that ignoring substitution 'can only understate' the layout's value; with substitution on, the recommended split can be significantly worse than the compared layout (-$70.27/week), because the optimiser leaves zero-gain coils empty that the comparison fills.
Six of seven seeded mutations survive: weekly scaling, sell-out percentage, extra-coil value, restock-table visit cost, simulated perishable waste and the max default are all unasserted.
Perishables can only be loaded in whole coils; there is no par level below coil capacity, which is how fresh food is stocked (sandwich 6/wk, 8/coil: $6.47/wk vs $9.15 at par 5).
No shelf-life check: the example stocks fresh sandwiches on a 7-day cycle and the restock table computes 10- and 14-day gaps for them with no warning.
When minimum coils fill the machine, the 'losing one coil' value is Infinity and renders '$Infinity a week'.
num() strips every comma, so a decimal-comma price '1,50' is read as 150 with no warning.
'30 is typical for snacks' substitution share has no cited source.

verdict: The engine is correct: an independent Python greedy and a brute force over 40 random machines match the dynamic program exactly, and the example's allocation, sell-out rates, restock table and Monte Carlo all recompute to the cent. It does not meet the bar. A blank Max coils field silently caps every product at 8 coils, so a drink machine is told to leave most coils empty while its best seller sells out every visit, with advice that the machine has too many coils; the README's claim that ignoring substitution 'can only understate' is false, and the tool can recommend a split that its own simulation shows earns $70 a week less than the comparison; fresh food cannot be given a par below coil capacity or a shelf-life limit; and six of seven seeded bugs, including one that cuts every weekly dollar figure by 12.5%, pass all 26 tests. Correctness, claims, fitness and domain 2, verification 1, completeness and craft 3.
